text:
I have reached the point where I have decided to cancel my Bark subscription because, for my industry, it simply does not provide value for money.

I run a home companionship and domiciliary care business, and leads in this category are extremely expensive. On average, it costs around 24 credits just to contact one customer. At approximately £1.88 per credit, buying £164 worth of credits only allows me to contact around four or five people.

The problem is that many of those leads never respond. When someone eventually does reply, it is often to say they are no longer looking for the service. Most of these conversations happen over the phone, so when I submit a credit review request, Bark asks me to provide evidence. They often tell me they were unable to verify the customer's response themselves and therefore require me to prove that the lead was no longer valid.

This is what I find most frustrating. If Bark cannot verify the validity of the leads on its own platform, how is a service provider expected to do so? I have found myself sending follow-up text messages to customers, asking them to confirm in writing that they are no longer looking for the service purely so I can request a refund for the credits I paid. Some customers reply, but most do not. It is unreasonable to expect providers to chase customers for evidence just to recover credits.

Over time, I estimate I have spent around £1,400 on Bark, in addition to paying the monthly subscription fee. Although I have secured two clients through the platform, the overall return has not justified the amount I have invested. The cost of the leads, combined with the difficulty of recovering credits for invalid leads, makes the platform far too expensive for my business.

I believe Bark should take greater responsibility for verifying leads before charging professionals and should operate a much fairer and more transparent credit refund process. Businesses should not have to prove something that the platform itself says it cannot verify.

Unfortunately, this will be the last month I purchase Bark credits. I cannot continue investing this amount of money for such poor value and an unfair refund process.
manual_complaint_themes: Poor ROI / expensive leads | Billing / refunds

text:
Bark has the potential to be a useful platform, and the website itself is easy to use. However, after purchasing multiple credit packages and Bark Premium, I haven't secured a single client.

The biggest issue isn't the number of enquiries—it's the quality and filtering. A significant proportion of leads either never respond after you've spent credits, or they're private individuals, students or very small businesses with extremely limited budgets. Many of the projects I saw were in the £250–£950 range, with some considerably lower.

For that reason, I think Bark currently works best for low to mid-skilled freelancers who are happy to take on smaller projects. If you're an established agency or a senior consultant whose projects typically start at several thousand pounds, the platform is much harder to justify commercially.

There are two improvements that I believe would make a huge difference:

• Require business enquiries to include a registered company name (verified where possible via Companies House filter) so providers can distinguish genuine businesses from speculative enquiries.

• Allow providers to filter leads by annual turnover, rather than just service category and location or size (a SME that does £100k revenue and one that does £700k will have much more regular and better budgeted work). Not every provider is targeting the same type of client, and the platform should reflect that.

I genuinely hope Bark continues to improve because the concept is strong. Better qualification and filtering would make it a much more valuable platform for established agencies and experienced professionals, not just freelancers competing for lower-value work.

text:
My Experience With Yelp Advertising – A Warning for Small Business Owners

I am sharing my experience so other small business owners can make informed decisions before signing up for Yelp advertising services.

I was contacted by a Yelp representative and was assisted with setting up an advertising account. During this process, I provided payment information. However, I was never provided a contract by mail, never received a signed agreement, and, to the best of my knowledge, was never emailed any advertising agreement or terms and conditions.

Yelp offered promotional advertising credits as part of the account setup. During the advertising period, I began receiving messages that I believed were not resulting in legitimate business opportunities. In several instances, messages would be received, but after responding, there was no further communication. This raised concerns for me regarding the quality of the leads being generated.

Because of these concerns, I made the decision to cancel my Yelp advertising account. I have documentation showing that the account was canceled, and Yelp’s own records acknowledge the cancellation date.

Despite the cancellation, I was later charged $863. I disputed the charge and attempted to resolve the matter directly with Yelp. Unfortunately, I was unable to obtain a satisfactory resolution through customer service.

I subsequently filed a complaint with my state’s Attorney General’s office. Yelp responded to the Attorney General’s inquiry, but I remained dissatisfied with the company’s position and explanation regarding the charges.

Throughout this process, I repeatedly requested clarification regarding the basis for the charges and any agreement authorizing them. My concern remains that I was charged after cancellation despite my understanding that the account had already been terminated.

I encourage any small business owner considering Yelp advertising to:

• Carefully review all advertising terms and conditions.
• Request copies of any agreements in writing.
• Save all emails, account records, and cancellation confirmations.
• Monitor billing statements closely.
• Document all communications with representatives.
• Keep records of cancellation dates and account activity.

This post reflects my personal experience and opinions based on my records and interactions. Other business owners may have different experiences. I encourage everyone to conduct their own research and maintain thorough documentation when entering into any advertising agreement.

Business Owner,
TTR TAX & NOTARY CO LLC

La société n'a pas fait appel à un maçon pour réparer les dégâts. Le crépi a été sommairement réparé par le menuisier, qui n'est pas du métier.
J'ai donc dû procéder moi-même aux finitions, notamment la peinture de l'encadrement.

Pour une prestation qui m'a coûté 1585 euros TTC (pose comprise), je m'attendais à une qualité et un service bien supérieurs.
Je suis très déçu et ne recommande pas ces entreprises.

text:
My Experience with Checkatrade Over the Last Six Months

I want to describe my experience with Checkatrade over the last six months and explain what I have personally experienced since joining.

There are several types of customers I have encountered through the platform.

First, we have people who supposedly need a job done remotely, sometimes even thousands of miles away from where you operate. While you are paying for your Checkatrade membership, you constantly have to contact these customers, arrange messages, make calls and spend your valuable time trying to organise the job.

However, sometimes they are actually looking for something else or, in my experience, some enquiries have appeared suspicious or potentially fraudulent. You contact the customer, call them or try to arrange the job, only to discover that the enquiry does not appear to be a genuine job.

When you are paying around £570 per month, you can see how quickly the costs can add up. Over a 12-month membership, that would be approximately £6,840 — nearly £7,000. Imagine spending nearly £7,000 over a year while receiving enquiries that may be unsuitable, unsuccessful or never turn into actual work.

That is a serious concern for a small business.

On the other hand, we have customers who post jobs because they want to compare 20 different companies. They can take up your time in the morning, but they don’t even have the time to send you a message or respond to you. Sometimes, after you have already spent time contacting them, they simply say that they have already found someone.

Then we have another type of customer who is looking for a service but is not actually sure whether they want to proceed. They are simply interested in comparing quotes and seeing how much the service will cost.

Even when they haven’t bought an item, have a house move coming up, or have a specific job they are supposedly looking for, sometimes they are still only looking around and comparing prices.

This is what I have personally experienced during my six months with Checkatrade.

The other issue is Checkatrade’s membership system. They are very busy promoting and selling memberships and encouraging people to pay for the service. However, when you actually experience the lead system, you realise that there is very little control over the quality of the enquiries being sent to you.

From my experience, you can be charged for a lead simply because the enquiry has been sent to you, regardless of whether it becomes a genuine job, whether the customer is serious, or whether the enquiry is suitable for your business.

That is the biggest problem I have experienced.

If I could give advice to another small business considering joining Checkatrade, I would seriously consider using the service on a shorter-term or credit basis rather than committing to a 12-month membership.

In my experience, Checkatrade was not what I understood it to be initially. I don’t feel that the reality of paying for individual leads and dealing with enquiries that may not become genuine jobs was made clear enough at the beginning.

Please do your research before joining. Think carefully before committing to a 12-month membership. Don’t assume every lead is a genuine customer ready to book.

This is my personal experience over the last six months, and I am sharing it so other businesses can make an informed decision before committing their time and money.

For me personally, I would stay away from it.

I am a professional builder and my experience with Bark has been extremely disappointing and costly.

Bark uses misleading practices to push professionals into spending credits without receiving real value. Credits are deducted simply by clicking “View details” or accidentally pressing “Contact”, especially on mobile where the buttons are placed extremely close together. One accidental click = money gone, with no confirmation step.

What is even more concerning is the use of very large “tender-style” opportunities, such as £10m–£60m+ Design & Build projects allegedly linked to public bodies (e.g. Crown Estate). These listings are clearly designed to look serious and high-value, but they have no place on a platform like Bark and are completely unrealistic for how real public procurement works.

These “big tenders” strongly encourage professionals to click out of curiosity or hope, only to immediately lose credits. In reality, such projects are procured through official frameworks and tender portals — not Bark. This feels deliberately misleading.

I have spent over £700 in credits without securing a single job. Many leads either never respond, are unsuitable once details are revealed, or appear to exist only to trigger credit charges.

This platform appears to make money from clicks and dark UX design, not from helping professionals win work. I strongly warn other builders and tradespeople: be extremely careful.

I would not recommend Bark to professionals who value transparency and fair business practices.

It will be a while before we dine here again: by that time, perhaps the owner will find competent servers.

My personal experience with Checkatrade has been extremely disappointing.

Last year, when work was quiet, I signed up because I believed it was a pay-as-you-go service. I was later charged £36 a month, which wasn’t what I believed I’d agreed to. I contacted them, asked to cancel, and my monthly fee was reduced to £0, so I genuinely believed my account had been closed.

Because I thought it was all over, I deleted the app and blocked their emails.

Fast forward 12 months, and I’ve suddenly started receiving two or three phone calls a day asking me to pay £36 a month because my account had automatically renewed. I had no idea this had happened.

I’ve contacted them repeatedly asking to cancel, but they’ve refused. After several stressful phone calls, the best they offered was to reduce the fee to £12 a month for a service I don’t want, don’t need, and won’t use.

To make matters worse, during a call with a member of the cancellations team today, I felt I was spoken to dismissively and even believed they were sniggering at me while I was trying to explain my situation. That only added to the frustration and stress of the whole experience.

This has been my personal experience, and I’m sharing it so other tradespeople can make sure they fully understand the terms, especially any automatic renewal conditions, before signing up.
